chunks.content: Introduction The incidence of EC is steadily rising, particularly among elderly women, posing significant challenges for clinical management due to age-related comorbidities, aggressive tumor biology, and reduced treatment tolerance [ , ]. Advanced age is a well-established negative prognostic factor, often associated with higher recurrence rates and cancer-related mortality despite standard radical hysterectomy with lymph node assessment [ , ]. In line with geriatric oncology research, we defined “elderly” as age ≥ 65 years, which is a widely accepted threshold in both clinical trials and epidemiological studies of EC. This age cutoff is recommended by organizations such as the World Health Organization and is commonly used in geriatric oncology to identify patients at higher risk of functional decline, comorbidities, and treatment-related toxicity. Although alternative cutoffs (e.g., ≥ 70 or ≥ 75 years) exist, the age of 65 years represents a common benchmark for identifying patients with increased vulnerability to treatment-related toxicity and worse cancer outcomes. This heterogeneity in outcomes underscores the critical need for robust, readily available prognostic biomarkers to improve risk stratification and personalize postoperative management for elderly EC patients. The tumor microenvironment and host systemic response, including nutrition and systemic inflammation, are closely related to cancer progression and treatment outcomes [ , ]. The GNRI, originally developed to assess nutritional risk in elderly hospitalized patients, has demonstrated significant prognostic value across various malignancies [ ]. This simple composite index, derived from serum albumin and body weight, reflects protein-energy malnutrition and skeletal muscle mass loss (sarcopenia), which are associated with worse treatment tolerance, increased postoperative complications, and impaired anti-tumor immunity [ ]. Concurrently, the systemic inflammatory response, mediated through various cytokines and cellular components, creates a favorable microenvironment for tumor proliferation, angiogenesis, and metastasis [ ]. Numerous inflammation-based scores have been studied in EC, but their prognostic values vary [ ]. More recently, the PIV has emerged as a novel, comprehensive biomarker that incorporates four key hematological parameters (neutrophils, platelets, monocytes, and lymphocytes) into a single formula, potentially providing a more complete reflection of the host’s immune-inflammatory status [ ]. Elevated PIV has demonstrated promising prognostic utility in several solid tumors, including colorectal, lung, and gastric cancers [ – ], with emerging evidence also supporting its prognostic value in other malignancies such as breast cancer and Merkel cell carcinoma [ , ]. Elderly EC patients represent a particularly vulnerable population where the interplay between malnutrition and inflammation is often pronounced and clinically significant [ ]. Age-related physiological decline, including anorexia of aging and sarcopenia, can predispose to nutritional deficiencies, while the tumor itself can promote a chronic inflammatory state through cytokine production and immune system modulation [ ]. This creates a vicious cycle that may accelerate disease progression and compromise treatment outcomes [ ]. Although GNRI and PIV have been studied independently in other cancer types, their combined prognostic power has not been investigated in EC, and their specific role in the elderly cohort remains largely unexplored [ – ]. Previous studies have typically examined nutritional and inflammatory markers separately, potentially overlooking their synergistic effect on patient outcomes [ ]. Furthermore, most existing prognostic models for EC have not adequately addressed the unique challenges faced by elderly patients, who often present with distinct tumor biology and host characteristics [ ]. This retrospective study, therefore, specifically aimed to address this gap by comprehensively evaluating the prognostic value of preoperative GNRI and PIV, both individually and in combination, in a cohort strictly limited to elderly patients (≥ 65 years) with EC undergoing radical surgery. While previous studies have reported the prognostic role of GNRI or PIV individually in various malignancies, including some gynecological cancers, few have focused specifically on the elderly EC population, in whom age-related physiological decline often leads to a pronounced interplay between malnutrition and chronic inflammation-a state sometimes termed “inflammaging”. We hypothesized that in this specific population, low GNRI and high PIV would be associated with aggressive clinicopathological characteristics and would independently predict worse overall survival, recurrence-free survival, and higher two-year recurrence rates. Furthermore, we postulated that the integration of these two host-specific factors would yield superior prognostic accuracy compared to using either marker alone or traditional tumor-centric factors, offering a simple, cost-effective, and clinically accessible tool for refining postoperative risk stratification and personalizing management strategies for this growing yet vulnerable patient subgroup. Materials and methods Study design and population We screened the medical records of elderly patients who underwent primary radical surgery for histologically proven EC at The Second Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University between February 2021 and November 2023. The study protocol complied with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. The protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of The Second Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University Hospital (Approval No.: 2022 − 207; Date of Approval: May 27, 2022), and the informed consent

refining postoperative risk stratification and personalizing management strategies for this growing yet vulnerable patient subgroup. Materials and methods Study design and population We screened the medical records of elderly patients who underwent primary radical surgery for histologically proven EC at The Second Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University between February 2021 and November 2023. The study protocol complied with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. The protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of The Second Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University Hospital (Approval No.: 2022 − 207; Date of Approval: May 27, 2022), and the informed consent was also obtained. The official ethics approval document is available upon request. Inclusion criteria were: (1) age ≥ 65 years; (2) pathologically confirmed endometrial carcinoma; (3) receiving radical surgery, which in the context of this study refers to comprehensive surgical staging, defined as at minimum total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TH + BSO), with or without pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph node assessment; (4) intact clinical records. Exclusion criteria included: (1) presence of synchronous other malignancies; (2) receipt of neoadjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy prior to surgery; (3) receipt of any immunotherapy prior to surgery or during the study period; (4) active infection, autoimmune diseases, or chronic inflammatory conditions that could significantly affect inflammatory markers; (5) incomplete preoperative laboratory data (within one week before surgery) required for calculating GNRI and PIV; (6) incomplete clinicopathological or follow-up data. A final cohort of 156 patients was included in the analysis. To explore potential age-related heterogeneity, we performed a sensitivity analysis by stratifying patients into two age subgroups: 65–74 years ( n = 102) and ≥ 75 years ( n = 54). The prognostic impact of GNRI and PIV remained consistent across both subgroups (all P < 0.05), supporting the robustness of our findings within the defined elderly population. Additionally, we conducted subgroup analyses based on FIGO stage to evaluate the prognostic value of the combined GNRI-PIV stratification within early-stage (Stage I/II, n = 120) and advanced-stage (Stage III/IV, n = 36) disease. In the early-stage subgroup, patients with low GNRI/high PIV (Group 1) had significantly worse 3-year OS (61.5% vs. 92.9% in high GNRI/low PIV group, P < 0.001) and higher 2-year recurrence rate (57.1% vs. 10.2%, P < 0.001). Among advanced-stage patients, the combined GNRI-PIV groups also showed distinct survival outcomes (3-year OS: 41.7% in Group 1 vs. 77.8% in Group 4, P = 0.008). These results indicate that the combined GNRI-PIV model can further refine risk stratification within both early and advanced FIGO stages. Surgical procedures All patients underwent comprehensive surgical staging, which included at minimum a total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TH + BSO). Pelvic lymph node dissection (PLND) was performed in 150 patients (96.2%), and para-aortic lymph node dissection (PALND) was performed in 48 patients (30.8%) based on preoperative risk assessment and intraoperative findings. Sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping was utilized in 22 patients (14.1%). Surgical approach (open, laparoscopic, or robotic) was selected based on patient characteristics and surgeon preference. Omentectomy was not routinely performed unless there was clinical suspicion of extra-uterine disease. The median operative time was 180 min (IQR 150–210), and estimated blood loss was recorded. The distribution of surgical extent (lymph node assessment: PLND, PALND, SLN mapping) and surgical approach (minimally invasive vs. open) did not differ significantly across GNRI-PIV groups (all P > 0.05). Data collection and definitions Demographic, clinical, surgical, and pathological data were meticulously extracted from electronic medical records. Collected variables included age, BMI, FIGO stage (2009 criteria, as this was the institutional standard during the majority of the study period and ensures consistency in pathological reporting), histology, grade, myometrial invasion, LVSI, lymph node status, extent of lymph node assessment (PLND, PALND, SLN mapping), surgical approach (open, laparoscopic, robotic), and postoperative adjuvant treatments (categorized as none, radiotherapy alone, chemotherapy alone, or combined chemoradiotherapy). Preoperative laboratory data, including complete blood count with differential and serum albumin, were collected within one week before surgery. Data on postoperative adjuvant therapy (including radiotherapy, chemotherapy, hormonal therapy, or combinations thereof) were also collected. Adjuvant therapy decisions were made based on multidisciplinary tumor board recommendations considering pathological risk factors. Calculation of GNRI and PIV The GNRI was calculated using the following formula: GNRI = (1.489 × serum albumin [g/L]) + (41.7 × (current body weight [kg] / ideal body weight [kg])). As per the original GNRI methodology, if the ratio of current body weight to ideal body weight exceeded 1, it was set to 1 to avoid overestimating nutritional status in overweight or obese individuals [ ]. The ideal body weight was derived from the Lorentz formula for women: Ideal weight (kg) = Height (cm) − 100 - ((Height (cm) − 150) / 2.5). Based on the formula of PIV = (neutrophil count × platelet count × monocyte count) /

following formula: GNRI = (1.489 × serum albumin [g/L]) + (41.7 × (current body weight [kg] / ideal body weight [kg])). As per the original GNRI methodology, if the ratio of current body weight to ideal body weight exceeded 1, it was set to 1 to avoid overestimating nutritional status in overweight or obese individuals [ ]. The ideal body weight was derived from the Lorentz formula for women: Ideal weight (kg) = Height (cm) − 100 - ((Height (cm) − 150) / 2.5). Based on the formula of PIV = (neutrophil count × platelet count × monocyte count) / lymphocyte count, PIV was calculated. All blood cell counts were expressed as 10⁹/L. The resulting PIV is a unitless ratio, with higher values indicating a more pronounced pro-inflammatory and immunosuppressive state. Follow-up and endpoints Patients were followed according to institutional guidelines: quarterly for the first 2 years, semi-annually for the next 3 years, and annually thereafter. Physical examination, serum cancer antigen 125 (CA-125) testing, and imaging were performed during the follow-up as clinically indicated. The primary endpoints were OS and RFS. Secondary endpoints included two-year recurrence rates. The 3-year OS endpoint was selected because it represents a clinically meaningful medium-term survival benchmark in endometrial carcinoma, especially in elderly patients with competing risks of mortality. The 2-year recurrence endpoint was chosen specifically to focus on early recurrence patterns, which are particularly relevant for aggressive disease biology and have been associated with worse long-term outcomes in endometrial carcinoma. Early recurrence (within 24 months) often reflects more aggressive tumor behavior and may necessitate intensified surveillance or adjuvant strategies. This endpoint differs from RFS in that it is a binary outcome (recurrence yes/no within 24 months) and does not incorporate death events, providing a distinct measure of early tumor aggressiveness. RFS referred to the interval from surgery to first recurrence or death from any cause. The interval from surgery to death from any cause was defined for OS. Event-free patients were censored at their last follow-up. The follow-up data were updated until March 2025, providing a minimum potential follow-up time of 16 months for all patients. Patients without an event (recurrence or death) at the last contact before March 2025 were censored at that date. Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS 26.0 and R 4.2.0. Categorical data are presented as n (%) and analyzed with chi-square or Fisher’s exact test. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median with interquartile range based on distribution normality, and compared using Student’s t-test or Mann-Whitney U test as appropriate. The 3-year OS and 2-year recurrence endpoints were selected as clinically meaningful benchmarks for medium-term survival and early recurrence in this elderly cohort, respectively. To determine optimal prognostic cutoffs for GNRI and PIV for predicting 3-year OS while appropriately handling censored survival data, we performed time-dependent ROC analysis at 36 months using the “timeROC” package in R, with the cutpoint selected based on the maximum Youden index. Patients were subsequently stratified into high and low groups based on these cutoffs (GNRI: 97.8, PIV: 292.3). It should be noted that these cutoffs were derived from the present cohort and are considered exploratory, requiring validation in external populations. Survival analysis was performed using Kaplan-Meier method with log-rank test. The proportional hazards assumption was tested using Schoenfeld residuals and was satisfied. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards models were used to identify independent prognostic factors. Variables with P < 0.1 in univariate analysis for the respective endpoint were considered for inclusion. The final multivariate model for each endpoint was constructed by including the two primary biomarkers (GNRI and PIV) and the most clinically relevant factors (FIGO stage and lymph node metastasis). To account for potential confounding, adjuvant therapy (categorized as none, radiotherapy alone, chemotherapy alone, or combined chemoradiotherapy) was forced into all multivariate models. No significant interaction was found between adjuvant therapy type and GNRI/PIV status regarding OS or RFS ( P for interaction > 0.05). The stability of the multivariate model coefficients was internally assessed using 1000 bootstrap resamples. Biomarker performance was compared using time-dependent ROC analysis with the DeLong test, and the discriminatory power of the combined model was assessed using Harrell’s C-index. All statistical tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Patients with low GNRI were significantly older, had lower BMI, and had more aggressive tumor features, including advanced FIGO stage, higher tumor grade, positive lymph node metastasis, and greater frequency of LVSI (all P < 0.05). Discussion Our study is the first to comprehensively evaluate the combined prognostic role of preoperative GNRI and PIV exclusively in a cohort of elderly (≥ 65 years) patients with EC undergoing radical surgery. Our findings robustly demonstrate that both biomarkers, reflecting distinct yet interconnected domains of host status (nutrition and systemic inflammation), are powerful independent predictors of OS, RFS, and early recurrence in this vulnerable population. Crucially, the novel combination of these easily accessible, preoperative markers provided superior risk stratification compared to clinicopathological factors alone, highlighting their potential to augment existing prognostic models. The core innovation of this research lies in demonstrating that a combined host-factor model, readily derivable from routine preoperative data, effectively stratifies risk specifically within the challenging context of geriatric EC. The prognostic significance of GNRI in our study aligns with growing evidence linking malnutrition to poor cancer outcomes [ , , ]. In elderly EC patients, nutritional status assumes even greater importance due to age-related physiological changes, including sarcopenia and anorexia of aging [ , ]. Our results extend previous findings by specifically focusing on the elderly population and demonstrating that GNRI not only predicts long-term survival but also early recurrence rates. The mechanisms underlying this association are multifactorial, including reduced treatment tolerance, impaired immune function, and metabolic alterations that may promote tumor progression [ , ]. The simplicity of GNRI calculation, based on routinely available parameters (albumin and weight), enhances its clinical applicability as a practical tool for identifying high-risk elderly EC patients who might benefit from preoperative nutritional assessment and targeted interventions, a consideration of particular importance in a population prone to sarcopenia and anorexia of aging. Similarly, the independent prognostic value of PIV underscores the critical role of systemic inflammation in EC progression. The simplicity of GNRI calculation, based on routinely available parameters (albumin and weight), enhances its clinical applicability as a practical tool for identifying high-risk elderly EC patients who might benefit from preoperative nutritional assessment and targeted interventions, a consideration of particular importance in a population prone to sarcopenia and anorexia of aging. Similarly, the independent prognostic value of PIV underscores the critical role of systemic inflammation in EC progression. PIV integrates key cellular components of the immune-inflammatory response: neutrophils and platelets that promote angiogenesis and metastasis; monocytes that differentiate into tumor-associated macrophages fostering an immunosuppressive microenvironment; and lymphocytes that are crucial for anti-tumor immunity [ , ]. An elevated PIV thus reflects enhanced pro-tumor inflammation and suppressed anti-tumor immunity. Our findings are consistent with studies in other malignancies [ – , ] and suggest that PIV may represent a more comprehensive indicator of the host’s immune status compared to simpler ratios like NLR or PLR, although direct comparative studies are warranted. The most significant contribution of our study is the demonstration of a powerful synergistic effect between nutritional status (GNRI) and systemic inflammation (PIV). The combined biomarkers effectively categorized patients into four distinct risk groups with markedly different survival outcomes and recurrence patterns. Patients with concurrent malnutrition (low GNRI) and high systemic inflammation (high PIV) exhibited the worst prognosis, with a strikingly high two-year recurrence rate of 65.8% and significantly inferior OS and RFS. This finding highlights the vicious cycle between these two conditions, often referred to as “inflammaging” and malnutrition-sarcopenia syndrome in the elderly [ , ]. From a pathophysiological perspective, malnutrition (reflected by low GNRI) leads to muscle wasting, reduced protein synthesis, and impaired immune cell function, while systemic inflammation (high PIV) promotes a pro-tumor microenvironment through cytokine release (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α), angiogenesis, and suppression of anti-tumor lymphocytes. Together, they create a state of chronic immune suppression and metabolic dysregulation that facilitates tumor progression, metastasis, and early recurrence. This pathological interplay can lead to functional decline, increased treatment toxicity, and accelerated disease progression through multiple mechanisms, including enhanced oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired tissue repair capacity [ , ]. Conversely, patients with good nutritional status and low inflammation (high GNRI/low PIV) demonstrated excellent outcomes, with a two-year recurrence rate of 9.6% and the most favorable long-term survival. Interestingly, patients in Group 3 (high GNRI/high PIV) exhibited an even lower early recurrence rate of 3.1%, suggesting that good nutritional status may profoundly mitigate the impact of systemic inflammation on early disease control, a hypothesis warranting further investigation. This suggests that a robust host defense mechanism, characterized by adequate nutritional reserves and balanced immune function, may effectively contain tumor progression even in elderly patients. The identification of this low-risk subgroup is particularly clinically relevant, as it might allow for treatment de-escalation strategies to avoid overtreatment and preserve quality of life in this vulnerable population, especially for those with early-stage disease. The superior prognostic performance of the combined GNRI-PIV model, as evidenced by higher AUC values in ROC analysis and high Harrell’s C-index, underscores its potential clinical utility. Critically, our incremental value analyses demonstrated that adding GNRI and PIV to a model based on established clinical factors (age, FIGO stage, grade, LNM, LVSI) significantly improved risk stratification, as reflected by the increase in C-index, IDI, and NRI (Table ). This composite model outperformed not only individual markers but also traditional prognostic factors, suggesting that it captures essential aspects of the host-tumor interaction that are not fully reflected by conventional staging systems. The integration of nutritional and inflammatory assessment provides a more holistic view of the patient’s biological status, which is especially valuable in elderly cancer patients where host factors significantly influence treatment outcomes [ , ]. Our findings have important clinical implications. The preoperative assessment of GNRI and PIV is inexpensive, reproducible, and based on routine blood tests and anthropometric measurements. This combination could be easily integrated into clinical practice to improve risk stratification for elderly EC patients. As a hypothesis-generating perspective derived from our retrospective data, the GNRI-PIV model may help generate testable hypotheses for future risk-adapted strategies. While these concepts require rigorous validation, we posit that for high-risk patients (low GNRI/high PIV), future prospective trials could investigate the potential benefit of interventions such as preoperative nutritional optimization, physical prehabilitation, or intensified adjuvant regimens. For low-risk patients (high GNRI/low PIV), the hypothesis of de-escalating adjuvant therapy or follow-up intensity to reduce treatment burden without compromising oncologic safety could also be explored. We must underscore that all these potential strategies are speculative, derived from an observational study, and must be prospectively tested in well-designed clinical trials before any change to standard practice can be contemplated. Several limitations of this study warrant acknowledgment. Firstly, its retrospective and single-center design introduces potential selection bias. Secondly, the sample size, though reasonable, is relatively modest, particularly for subgroup analyses and for advanced-stage (FIGO III/IV) patients ( n = 36, 23.1%), which limits the statistical power and generalizability of findings within this high-risk subgroup. Third, the lack of an external validation cohort limits the generalizability of our cutoff values and model performance; it is important to emphasize that the proposed GNRI-PIV model and the derived thresholds (GNRI: 97.8; PIV: 292.3) are exploratory and require validation in independent, multi-institutional cohorts before clinical application. Future multicenter studies are needed to validate the combined GNRI-PIV model. The cutoff values identified in this study (GNRI: 97.8; PIV: 292.3) were derived from our specific elderly EC cohort and may differ from those reported in studies of younger patients or other cancer types. For instance, previous studies in different malignancies have reported varying GNRI cutoffs (often around 92–98) and PIV cutoffs (ranging from 200 to 400), reflecting population-specific and disease-specific variations. Therefore, while our cutoffs are statistically optimized for our cohort, their external validity needs confirmation in independent elderly EC populations. Future validation studies should also explore whether age-specific or disease-stage-specific cutoffs further improve prognostic accuracy. Fourth, the median follow-up time of 28 months is relatively short for a malignancy with a potentially long natural history like EC; longer follow-up is needed to confirm the long-term prognostic value of these markers. Although we focused on early recurrence (2-year) and medium-term survival (3-year OS/RFS), the relatively short follow-up remains a limitation for assessing very long-term outcomes such as 5-year or 10-year survival. We acknowledge that the survival curves presented may appear notably regular. This pattern likely reflects the concentrated timeline of events within this relatively short, defined follow-up period for a cohort with clear stratification by strong prognostic factors (GNRI and PIV), rather than irregular long-term follow-up data. Fifth, the cut-off values for GNRI and PIV were determined based on our cohort and may require external validation. Sixth, we lacked data on molecular subtypes of endometrial carcinoma (e.g., POLE mutation, MMR status, p53 abnormality), which are increasingly recognized as important prognostic and predictive factors. The absence of this molecular information is a significant limitation, as these subtypes are known to be associated with both tumor aggressiveness and the tumor immune microenvironment, potentially confounding the relationship between host inflammatory markers (PIV) and outcomes. Their omission may therefore introduce residual confounding and limits our ability to assess the independent prognostic value of GNRI and PIV beyond modern molecular risk stratification. Seventh, while we adjusted for the broad category of adjuvant therapy in our multivariate models and found no significant interaction with biomarker status, we lacked detailed data on specific regimens, doses, duration, and patient compliance. The heterogeneity in adjuvant therapy intensity could potentially confound outcomes, and although our adjustments provide some reassurance, residual confounding due to these unmeasured variations cannot be entirely excluded. Additionally, other potential confounders such as comprehensive geriatric assessment data (comorbidity burden, frailty, performance status), surgical approach (minimally invasive vs. open), and detailed lymph node assessment strategy (e.g., sentinel lymph node biopsy alone vs. systematic lymphadenectomy) were not available for adjustment in our analysis. The absence of these variables may lead to residual confounding. Finally, our study is exploratory, and the proposed biomarkers and their exploratory cut-off values require validation in larger, prospective, multi-institutional cohorts that incorporate molecular classification and data on supportive interventions before they can be recommended for routine clinical use. The integration of nutritional (GNRI) and inflammatory (PIV) profiling into preoperative assessment aligns with the growing emphasis on geriatric assessment and personalized medicine in oncology [ , ]. Recent guidelines underscore the importance of evaluating and addressing nutritional deficits and systemic inflammation to optimize outcomes in older cancer patients. Furthermore, as the prognostic value of PIV gains validation across diverse malignancies, including metastatic colorectal cancer, its application in gynecologic cancers warrants further exploration. Our findings provide a rationale for future trials to investigate whether targeted interventions—such as preoperative immunonutrition, anti-inflammatory strategies, or tailored adjuvant therapy based on GNRI-PIV stratification—can improve survival in high-risk elderly EC patients [ – ]. Conclusion In conclusion, this study establishes that preoperative GNRI and PIV are potent, independent, and cost-effective prognostic biomarkers in elderly patients with endometrial carcinoma undergoing radical surgery.

This simple composite model may help clinicians recognize patients at the highest risk of recurrence and death, thereby facilitating personalized treatment planning, optimizing adjuvant therapy decisions, and guiding nutritional and supportive interventions. Future prospective studies are warranted to validate our findings and to explore whether interventions targeting these modifiable factors can ultimately improve survival outcomes in this vulnerable patient population.
